title: Mexico at the OAS: “Categorically” Rejects the Term Narcoterrorism for Lacking an Agreed Definition
author: Arturo Sánchez Jiménez
content:
_This article by[Arturo Sánchez
Jiménez](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Arturo%20S%C3%A1nchez%20Jim%C3%A9nez)
originally appeared in the [November 20, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/11/20/politica/expresa-
mexico-profunda-preocupacion-en-la-oea-por-convocatoria-al-tiar), Mexico's
premier left wing daily newspaper._

Mexico rejected this Friday at the Organization of American States (OAS),
“with deep concern,” the convening of the consultative body of the Inter-
American Treaty of Reciprocal Assistance (TIAR) to confront transnational
organized crime. It warned that prioritizing a collective defense mechanism
that emerged from the Cold War “could create a scenario of greater violence in
which we all lose.”

At an extraordinary session of the OAS Permanent Council, Mexico’s permanent
representative, Alejandro Encinas, urged against establishing “an automatic
link” between organized crime and terrorism, because they are distinct
phenomena with their own legal frameworks.

The resolution, backed by **14 of the 18 TIAR member states that voted** ,
proposes examining actions “that do not involve the use of armed force”
against cartels. Brazil and Uruguay voted against it; Mexico, which gave
notice of withdrawal from the treaty in 2002, could not vote.

Encinas “categorically” rejected the term narcoterrorism because it lacks an
agreed definition. He said that the unilateral designation of a criminal group
as terrorist “does not change international rules on the use of force or
authorize military operations in the territory of other states,” and that only
the United Nations Security Council can make that determination.

He recalled that the first time TIAR was invoked was against Guatemala’s
“democratic and legitimately elected” government, “using the same argument
being advanced today,” an episode that ended with the US intervention that
overthrew Jacobo Árbenz. He added that the Malvinas War in 1982 exposed the
treaty’s inability to act, and that its most recent invocation, in 2019 amid
the Venezuelan crisis, showed the risk of treating an internal conflict as a
matter of regional security.

> “Security priorities cannot be subordinated to political considerations and
> the strategies of third countries,” he maintained. He placed on record that
> the decision “does not reflect the will of all members of the organization”
> and warned that the proposal “brings us closer to a point of no return where
> the OAS puts its mission and its future at risk.”

“**Drug trafficking does not originate south of the United States** ,” he
emphasized. He described it as a threat sustained by drug demand, arms
trafficking and a financial chain with global reach, and called for addressing
consumer markets, sources of weapons supplies and the financial systems that
sustain the cartels.

He recalled that the OAS already has bodies for cooperation, such as the
Secretariat for Multidimensional Security and the Inter-American Drug Abuse
Control Commission (CICAD), and reiterated Mexico’s willingness to strengthen
**intelligence sharing and police and judicial cooperation** , with respect
for each state’s sovereignty.
